Shares of Meta Platforms Inc (NASDAQ:META) tanked in early trading on Thursday, despite the company reporting upbeat third-quarter results.

Here are some key analyst takeaways:

  • Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian maintained a Neutral rating, while raising the price target from $700 to $730.
  • TD Cowen analyst John Blackledge reiterated a Buy rating, while cutting the price target from $865 to $830.
  • Scotiabank analyst Nat Schindler reaffirmed a Sector Perform rating, while lifting the price target from $600 to $650.
  • Rosenblatt Securities analyst Barton Crockett reiterated a Buy rating, while raising the price target from $886 to $900.
  • KeyBanc Capital Markets analyst Justin Patterson maintained an Overweight rating, while lifting the price target from $900 to $905.
  • Cantor Fitzgerald analyst Deepak Mathivanan reaffirmed an Overweight rating, while raising the price target from $840 to $860.
  • Guggenheim Securities analyst Michael Morris reiterated a Buy rating and price target of $850.
  • Needham analyst Laura Martin reaffirmed a Hold rating on the stock.
  • Benchmark analyst Mark Zgutowicz maintained a Hold rating on the stock.

Check out other analyst stock ratings.

Wedbush: Meta’s third-quarter results and fourth-quarter guidance were broadly ahead of expectations, Arounian said in a note. He added, however, that management did not provide additional visibility into cost and capex outlooks for 2027, while indicating plans to continue investing "aggressively."

The strong AI product release cadence, especially the "big ambitions for Muse," is likely to require a significant increase in compute capacity in 2027, the analyst stated. He raised the 2027 capex estimate from $210 billion to $249 billion.

TD Cowen: Meta’s revenue grew 26.1% year-on-year and came in 2% higher than consensus, Blackledge said. While the company’s ad revenue beat reflected strength across all regions, time spent per user on Instagram and Facebook Reels grew by double digits in the quarter, he added.

Management’s fourth-quarter revenue guidance of $73-$76 billion was 3% above consensus, the analyst stated. "We expect META to continue to drive engagement & ad performance through LLM powered user & content understanding," he further wrote.

Scotiabank: Meta’s third-quarter results reflected continued core ad strength, Schindler said. He added, however, that Muse’s path to profitability depends on "a substantial reduction in serving costs and creating a new transaction-oriented revenue stream that requires changing consumer and business behavior."

The company plans to invest hundreds of billions of dollars, beginning as early as fall of 2026, the analyst stated. Management indicated that an equity raise may be necessary for their business plans, he noted.

Rosenblatt Securities: The third-quarter results showed that Meta’s AI-driven ad growth story remains "intact," Crockett said.

Revenues grew 26% year-on-year to $64.6 billion, a slight deceleration from the second quarter’s 28% pace, the analyst stated. The company’s fourth-quarter guidance suggests revenue growth of nearly 27%, despite incremental currency headwind, "with AI credited for driving the growth by increasing engagement and return on ad spend," he added.

KeyBanc Capital Markets: Meta’s reported earnings of $3.83 per share, missing consensus estimate of $5.29 per share, Patterson said. This included $9.9 billion of legal expenses related to the company’s mental health settlement, excluding which earnings would have been reported at $7.40 per share, he added.

Meta’s ad revenue continues to benefit from AI initiatives, the analyst stated. He expects AI product momentum to support low-to-mid-20% revenue growth through 2028, offsetting some of the incremental capex.

Cantor Fitzgerald: Engagement trends in both Facebook and Instagram reached record levels, driven by strong growth in video, Mathivanan said. Management expressed confidence in strong revenue growth through the year, he added.

Muse reached over 10 million new accounts, with daily retention rates near 25%, the analyst stated. "We think the company is carrying plenty of momentum with Muse," he further wrote.

Guggenheim Securities: Meta’s third-quarter revenue and operating profit came in higher than Street expectations, Morris said in a note. He added that the fourth-quarter guidance and preliminary 2027 commentary "were incrementally positive."

More than 25% of Muse users made an average purchase above $200, the analyst stated. Management is pursuing monetization of Muse "sooner than its normal playbook, with Muse revenue per user expected to exceed the existing Family of Apps level (several hundred dollars annually per U.S. user)," he further wrote.

Needham: Analyst Laura Martin recommended investors to "stay on the sidelines," citing:

  • Meta has indicated the need for "hundreds of billions of dollars" for AI investments.
  • Nonvoting stock split implies the company could raise around $100 billion worth of equity in the first half of 2027.
  • Muse is in early stages, while Apple Inc (NASDAQ:AAPL), Alphabet Inc (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Amazon.com Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN), Anthropic, and OpenAI "will each have agents, and some will be more trusted by consumers."

Benchmark: Meta’s gross margin of 79.3% missed consensus by around 80 basis points (bps), despite the revenue beat, Zgutowicz said.

Depreciation does not explain the gross margin miss as COGS (cost of goods sold) grew by $2.04 billion sequentially, while total D&A (depreciation and amortization) rose only $80 million, the analyst stated. This means at least $1.24 billion of the increase was cash cost, he noted.

META Price Action: Shares of Meta’s had declined by 8.02% to $641.55 at the time of publication on Thursday.

Wall Street is heavily selling tech and AI-linked stocks on Thursday. Homebuilders are seeing one of the best rallies in months.

Both moves have the same cause. Investors are pulling money out of artificial-intelligence trades and buying Treasuries on fears that AI spending may not hold up beyond next year.

As a result, the 10-year yield fell 17 basis points to 4.95%, slipping below 5% for the first time in about a month.

The 2-year yield also dropped 17 basis points to 4.63%, while the 30-year eased 13 basis points to 5.28%.

US 10-year Treasury yield, daily chart. Source: TradingView

Homebuilder ETFs Soar as Yields Pullback, Tech Slides

The iShares U.S. Home Construction ETF (BATS:ITB) jumped 4.5%, on track for its best session since June 24. The State Street SPDR S&P Homebuilders ETF (NYSE:XHB) gained 2.9%.

Tech moved the other way.

The State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE:XLK) fell 3.3%, and the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) lost 2.9%. Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) slid nearly 8% on worries about its AI spending.

Read Also: Meta Tumbles 6% on AI Spending Fears, 10-Year Yield Falls Below 5%: Stock Market Today

Homebuilders Were Priced for the Worst

The rebound comes from a very low base.

Earlier this week, Benzinga reported that the NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index fell to 29 in October, its lowest reading since June 2012 and below the April 2020 low.

In addition, 43% of builders cut prices this month, the highest share since 2020. The 30-year mortgage rate averaged 7.40% in the week to Oct. 15, according to Freddie Mac.

Stocks reflected that gloom. On Oct. 14, the ratio between XHB and the S&P 500 closed at its lowest level since April 2020.

Read Also: Homebuilder Sentiment Hits 2012 Lows As Stocks Trade Like They Did During COVID-19 Pandemic

The AI Hedge Is Playing Out

Last week, 22V Research analyst Dennis DeBusschere argued that homebuilders could work as a hedge against an AI spending slowdown.

His reasoning was that the AI investment boom has kept growth and 10-year yields high, which keeps buyers away from new homes. Consequently, a drop in AI spending would push yields lower and help housing.

Thursday’s session follows that script.

“The knee jerk reaction has been outperformance in Banks, Retail, Small caps, housing and Transports on AI buildout concern days,” DeBusschere said in a Thursday note.

However, he does not expect a quick rescue from the Federal Reserve, which meets next week.

“Our view will be that the Fed will be slow to react to AI uncertainty,” he said.

He added that the risk of an escalation in the Iran war after the midterm elections complicates the picture.

Ten Real-Estate Stocks Rallying as Yields Fall

Among the largest builders, Lennar Corp. (NYSE:LEN) rose 7.6%, while D.R. Horton Inc. (NYSE:DHI) and PulteGroup Inc. (NYSE:PHM) gained 5.4% and 4.4%.

REITs Are Barely Joining in

Commercial real estate tells a different story.

The State Street Real Estate Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE:XLRE) rose just 0.7%, and CBRE Group Inc. (NYSE:CBRE) fell 3%.

That keeps Thursday’s move in perspective. A 10-year yield below 5% eases pressure on mortgage rates, but one session does not undo two months of rising borrowing costs.

The Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares (NYSE:SOXL) plunged almost 20% on Thursday, hitting a six-month low as surging oil prices, concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) financing and a broader technology selloff rattled semiconductor investors.

Read Also: Dell Stock Drops in Tech Sell-Off: Profit-Taking Hits AI Server Giant

SOXL was among the most actively traded ETFs during midday trading Thursday, with shares falling to levels last seen in April. The selloff extended across the semiconductor sector, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH) dropping around 5.8% and the iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) tumbling more than 6.5%. Both funds hit fresh three-month lows.

Why SOXL’s Losses Are So Severe

Unlike traditional semiconductor ETFs, SOXL targets 300% of the daily performance of its benchmark index before fees and expenses. That leverage can magnify both gains and losses. The fund’s objective applies to a single trading day, not longer holding periods.

Consequently, a broad sector selloff can translate into a substantially larger decline for SOXL, making it particularly vulnerable when semiconductor stocks face simultaneous macroeconomic and AI-related headwinds.

Thursday’s plunge puts the spotlight on whether investors will treat the selloff as a buying opportunity or continue reducing exposure to one of the market’s most volatile AI-linked trades.

Technical Talk

SOXL shares were down 19.76% at $82.83 at the time of publication on Thursday, according to Benzinga Pro data. The significant decline reflects broader market pressures impacting the semiconductor sector, which has faced volatility amid changing economic conditions and investor sentiment.

The current price is notably below both key moving averages, indicating a bearish trend that suggests a lack of upward momentum in the short to medium term. The substantial gap from these averages highlights the challenges the ETF faces in regaining investor confidence and establishing a more stable price trajectory.

Trading volume on Thursday reached 140.3 million shares, suggesting heightened activity as investors reacted to market developments. SOXL was also the most actively traded fund on Thursday.

Read Also: Marvell Feels Supply Chain Bottlenecks Pressure, Stock Drops Amid Tech Sell-Off

Oil Shock Fans Wall Street’s Worries

President Donald Trump blamed Iran for the surge in oil prices, alleging in a Truth Social post that Tehran was fabricating attacks and deliberately pushing prices higher ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

Brent crude futures expiring in December rose 2.3% to above $111 per barrel, while December West Texas Intermediate futures gained 1.4%.

The broader market weakened as investors assessed the implications of higher energy prices. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:SPY) fell more than 1%, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100, lost around 3%.

For semiconductor stocks, persistent energy-price pressures could add to concerns about inflation, interest rates and the cost of financing capital-intensive AI infrastructure.

Jensen Huang’s Funding Warning Hits AI Stocks

Fresh concerns about AI investment added to the pressure.

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC that demand for neocloud computing providers was exceptionally strong, but access to working capital was becoming a bottleneck.

Nvidia shares fell more than 4.3% in midday trading. Meanwhile, semiconductor companies Coherent Corp (NYSE:COHR), Entegris Inc (NASDAQ:ENTG), Lam Research Corp (NASDAQ:LRCX) and Lattice Semiconductor Corp (NASDAQ:LSCC) recorded double-digit declines.

The pressure also spread to AI infrastructure providers. CoreWeave Inc (NASDAQ:CRWV) dropped nearly 9%, hitting a fresh 17-month low and falling below $60 for the second time that week. IREN Ltd. (NASDAQ:IREN) slid below $25 to a fresh 13-month low.

The Roundhill Memory ETF (BATS:DRAM) also fell almost 6%, hitting a new three-month low.

Michael Burry once again took aim at the AI spending boom on Thursday with a song predicting Big Tech’s trillion-dollar data centers will crumble into obsolescence.

In a post on his Substack, "Cassandra Unchained", Burry shared a track he said was written by a friend of the newsletter, calling it "brilliant" and "extremely well-done." He also uploaded the song to his YouTube channel and published the full lyrics.

A GPU Arms Race Set to Music

The song is told from the point of view of an AI model. Over several verses, the narrator watches companies pour concrete, lay fiber and buy land for data centers, then predicts the facilities will become obsolete as models grow more efficient. 

A refrain built around the word "compression" runs throughout. 

"[Compression] I’m the algorithm watching empires fall

[Compression] Turns out you didn’t need it all

[Compression] Every data center every rack every gpu

[Compression] they bought was solving for a problem that I already solved

[Compression] This is not a war,

This is just math."

Read Also: Meta Bulls Beware: Bond Market Sends Its Loudest Warning on Zuckerberg's Borrowing Binge

The lyrics take aim at Big Tech valuations, too. One verse argues the largest companies hold their worth mainly because customer data sits trapped inside proprietary systems, and suggests AI will soon be able to pull it out. Another compares the rush to buy GPUs to a nuclear arms race.

"I’m watching humans build for futures that I’ve already seen. They’re buying GPUs like nuclear weapons in an arms race, but the war’s already over they just haven’t seen my face," the lyrics state.

Burry closed his post with a question: "Quite an earworm, no?"

See More: Top Value Stocks

Burry Puts His Money Where His Mouth Is

Lighthearted delivery aside, the song’s message lines up with bets Burry has held for months.

Burry has held various bearish positions against Tesla Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA), Caterpillar Inc. (NYSE:CAT), Applied Materials Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT) the iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX), Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) and more.

Burry has been sounding alarms on chipmakers for even longer. Back in November 2025 he called Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), the Cisco equivalent of the current AI boom, a reference to Cisco Systems Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) and its collapse after the dot-com bubble burst. 

Big Tech shows no interest in slowing down. Total 2026 spending plans from the biggest hyperscalers topped $700 billion, according to Reuters, and the figure keeps climbing. Much of the money flows from Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META).  

Burry’s song makes the opposite bet. In its telling, every rack and every GPU is aimed at a problem AI will soon solve on its own.

Walmart Inc. (NASDAQ:WMT) is up 16.2% in October, on track for its best month since 1999.

And it is not alone.

Toothpaste, laundry detergent and soda are beating artificial intelligence on Wall Street this month.

By a wide margin.

The Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLP) is up 11.3% in October, heading for its best month since it launched in December 1998.

Meanwhile, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) is roughly flat, and the Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLK) has lost 6.9%. Chipmakers, as tracked by the iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX), have tumbled over 15%.

That puts staples about 11 percentage points ahead of the S&P 500 in a single month. In the fund’s 27-year history, only April 2022 produced a gap that wide.

So why are investors loading up on shampoo and cereal? And more importantly, are they seeing trouble coming?

Walmart Inc. monthly price change. Source: TradingView

The AI Trade Is Losing Its Grip

On Thursday, Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) fell about 8% on worries about its artificial intelligence spending. As a result, XLK dropped 3.4%, while XLP rallied 2.7%.

The 10-year Treasury yield fell about 17 basis points to 4.95%, its biggest one-day drop since Aug. 2, 2024.

Read Also: Meta Tumbles 6% on AI Spending Fears, 10-Year Yield Falls Below 5%: Stock Market Today

The exit started earlier.

Bank of America clients sold a record $14.8 billion of individual U.S. stocks in the week through Oct. 16.

“Clients sold stocks in 8 of 11 sectors led by Tech (2nd biggest outflows ever),” Bank of America equity quant strategist Jill Carey Hall said in a Bank of America Global Research report.

Staples were among the few sectors clients bought.

Defensives Can Get Crowded Too

Bank of America’s equity derivatives team, which includes strategist Abhinandan Deb, does not see the start of a tech crash.

The strategists described the AI selloff as “a largely positioning-driven hiccup on the fringes of the AI trade rather than evidence of secular weakness in the core,” in a report this week.

“US equities continue to rotate sharply in times of stress rather than rupture, with the recent outperformance of defensives vs tech historically extreme,” they said.

That rotation has its own risks.

“While seemingly paradoxical, defensives like healthcare and staples now sit among the highest BRI pockets of the market,” analysts added, referring to the bank’s Bubble Risk Indicator.

The buying among staples has been across the board.

Procter & Gamble Has Not Had a Month Like This Since 1998

Procter & Gamble Co. (NYSE:PG) rose 5.9% on Thursday after its fiscal first-quarter results.

The maker of Tide and Gillette is up 14.6% in October, on pace for its best month since October 1998, when it jumped 24.7%.

Core earnings rose 1% to $2.00 per share, net sales climbed 4% to $23.28 billion, and volumes grew 2.4%. The company also kept its fiscal 2027 core earnings outlook.

Still, P&G expects about $1.4 billion in after-tax commodity cost headwinds this fiscal year. Its chief financial officer said those pressures will be materially higher in the second quarter and second half because of oil prices.

Read Also: QUICK SPARK: Procter & Gamble Stock Eyes Best Day Since 2020 – The Rally Is Hiding Something Bigger

What Happened the Last Times Staples Ran This Far Ahead

Five of the seven earlier months came in 2000 and 2001, as investors fled the dot-com winners before a recession that began in March 2001.

The S&P 500 was lower a year later in five of the seven cases.

However, there is one key difference.

In every earlier case, the S&P 500 itself fell, by 1.6% to 9.5%. This October, SPY is flat and sits about 2.5% below the record intraday high it hit this month. In other words, money is rotating inside a market near its peak.

The closest match is recent. In February 2026, XLP gained 7.8% while SPY slipped 0.9%. Six months later, SPY was up 11.8%.

Prediction Markets Do Not See a Recession Yet

Polymarket traders see a 7.5% chance of a U.S. recession by the end of 2026 and a 35% chance by the end of 2027.

What the record month does show is how much investors want protection from the AI trade. The last time that urge was this strong, in 2000 and 2001, a bear market and a recession followed.

news.headline: Walmart’s Best Month Since 1999 Leads a Record Staples Rally: Is This a Warning Sign?
news.summary: Walmart is on track for its best month since 1999 as XLP heads for a record October. Past staples surges like this often came before weaker markets.

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) saw such strong demand for its Muse AI agent that the company’s Muse app did something now only accomplished 12 times in the United States. Here’s a look at the history made and what happened the other times the feat was accomplished.

Meta’s Muse Hits 10 Million in 40 Days

Meta currently has a hit on its hands with Muse, which recently passed the 10 million download milestone in the United States.

This marks the 12th time an app has hit the milestone in the United States in only 40 days, according to data from Sensor Tower.

The app has passed 10.2 million downloads, and as a potential sign of Muse’s strength, the rise in downloads comes as ChatGPT app installs in the U.S. have fallen 25%, according to Sensor Tower.

Muse was a big part of Meta’s recent quarterly results and commentary, and analysts are excited about the monetization opportunities.

One of the big questions is if the momentum for downloads will continue, and for that we look at the list of apps that previously reached the milestone.

Read Also: Meta Posts Q3 Double Beat: 'We're Seeing Velocity Across the Board'

10 Million in 40 Days Club

Sensor Tower said Meta’s Muse is the 12th app to reach the 10 million downloads-in-40-days milestone. We don’t know the full list, but TechCrunch reports that Muse is only the third non-gaming app to reach the milestone.

The other non-gaming apps to hit the milestone are Meta’s Threads, which hit it last in July 2023, and Disney+, the streaming app from The Walt Disney Company (NYSE:DIS).

Games that hit the milestone include "Fortnite," "PUBG Mobile," and "Pokemon Go."

Those games remain available today, though their download growth has slowed since their launch peaks.

The question for Meta is whether Muse can sustain that early momentum.

Threads hit the milestone in July 2023 and now has over 500 million monthly active users globally, but in the United States that total is estimated closer to 34 million.

Despite its global user base, Threads’ U.S. audience remains a fraction of its worldwide total.

Disney no longer breaks out its subscriber figures, but it has more than 59 million in the United States and Canada. Disney+ launched its app in November 2019.

For some of these apps, they hit 10 million downloads quickly, then growth slowed.

For Meta, the key will be to keep gaining new Muse users while also monetizing the ones it has.

SCHD ETF Price and Inflows are Rising

Billionaire investor Bill Ackman says Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) has the financial firepower to fund its massive artificial intelligence ambitions, pointing to roughly $82 billion in cash and securities as investors punish the company over surging spending.

“They’ve got 80 billion of cash on the balance sheet, they have no net leverage,” Ackman told CNBC Thursday.

“They could finance whatever they want to do with a turn or two of financial leverage and remain a very strong investment grade company,” he said.

Meta shares fell nearly 8% Thursday after the company raised the lower end of its 2026 capital expenditure forecast to $135 billion, retaining the $145 billion upper limit.

Ackman said the stock was up roughly 5% when he went to sleep on a flight, only to be down 6.5% before his interview.

“These are just short-term traders moving the stock around,” he said.

Meta’s Cash-Generating Power

Meta has spent nearly $86 billion building out its infrastructure in the first nine months of 2026. Remarkably, its business generated almost $97 billion in operating cash flow over the same period, enough to cover that spending and leave roughly $11 billion in free cash flow.

Even after that spending, Meta still ended September with $82.45 billion in cash and marketable securities, although it also carried nearly $81 billion in long-term debt.

The pace of spending is beginning to test that financial strength. Capital expenditure exceeded operating cash flow by $2.12 billion in the third quarter, raising questions about how much more Meta can spend before it needs additional financing.

But Ackman believes that investment is already paying off.

“They’ve proven that AI is helping them accelerate their business,” he said, calling Meta “extremely well positioned” in AI agents.

Third-quarter revenue climbed 26% to $64.6 billion, with AI improvements helping Meta’s advertising operations.

Why Meta Is Preparing to Raise More Money

Even so, Meta is preparing additional financing options.

An October 21 regulatory filing revealed that management expects substantial future capital needs, while an independent board committee warned that borrowing at the scale contemplated could damage its credit ratings.

That raises questions about how far Meta can expand its borrowing, even as Ackman argues it could comfortably take on more debt.

The company plans to introduce nonvoting Class C shares, allowing it to raise equity without diluting CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s voting control.

Ackman said Meta’s materials indicated Zuckerberg would have to sell substantial amounts of stock to pay California’s proposed billionaire wealth tax if it passes. The new shares would allow him to do so without surrendering control.

According to the filing, Zuckerberg agreed to remain a resident of California, or wherever Meta is headquartered, for eight years.

Ackman also argued that departures by wealthy residents would prevent the tax from raising its intended revenue.

On Polymarket, traders put the probability of the tax passing at 23% Thursday, with approximately $3.94 million traded.

Meta’s third-quarter earnings beat did little to stop the selloff, but Ackman remains convinced investors are overlooking its strength.

“This remains an incredibly undervalued stock and that’s why we own it,” he said.

An October Crash

October has a reputation for market turmoil, known as the ‘October Effect,’ and it rests on some of the worst crashes in market history.

On Thursday, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) pushed back against warnings that proposed billionaire wealth tax could drive wealthy residents out of the state after Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) (NASDAQ:META) struck a deal to keep CEO Mark Zuckerberg in California for eight years.

Ro Khanna Challenges Newsom, Sergey Brin Over Wealth Tax

Khanna took to X to argue that Zuckerberg’s arrangement undermines claims that billionaires would flee California if voters approve Proposition 40, a proposed one-time 5% tax on the state’s billionaires.

"Looks like billionaires will stay and figure out a way to pay the tax," Khanna wrote, adding that the measure could fund health care for children from low-income families.

"Gavin, can you and Sergey Brin stop with your fear-mongering of a billionaire exodus?" he asked, referring to Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) and Sergey Brin, co-founder of Alphabet Inc.’s (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Google.

How Meta’s Deal Could Help Zuckerberg Pay the Tax

According to a Wednesday filing, Meta plans to issue a new class of non-voting Class C shares to Zuckerberg in January 2027.

The arrangement would let him sell some shares to cover a potential multibillion-dollar tax bill without directly sacrificing his voting control of the company.

Zuckerberg, whose net worth is estimated at around $230 billion as per Bloomberg data, had reportedly considered moving his primary residence outside California over concerns about the proposed tax.

Under the agreement, he has committed to remaining a California resident, or living wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, for eight years.

The proposal remains uncertain, with political analysts questioning whether it will pass. California is home to as many as 250 billionaires with a combined fortune exceeding $2 trillion, Reuters reported.

Bernie Sanders Backs Tax As Critics Warn of Exodus

Khanna’s position aligns with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who argued last month that the tax could preserve health coverage for 3 million residents. Sanders also accused billionaires of spending $229 million to oppose the measure.

However, economist Peter Schiff has warned that the tax could prompt wealthy entrepreneurs to leave California, potentially forcing asset sales and weakening the state’s tax base.

Newsom opposes California’s proposal while supporting a federal wealth tax approach.

James Thorne, Chief Market Strategist at Wellington Altus, argued Thursday that investors may be misreading the pullback in artificial intelligence stocks, saying the correction could ultimately help extend the AI boom.

Why a Pullback Could Help

AI-linked stocks led Thursday’s tech selloff, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 falling 2.90%.

In a post on X, Thorne said it was a “natural, healthy correction” that was overdue and argued that a short-term downturn could keep the boom from “collapsing under its own weight.”

Lower valuations, tougher credit scrutiny and slower construction impose discipline, he said, stretching investment over more years and easing the inflationary pressure of a concentrated spending surge.

Falling share prices, he pointed out, are “not falling demand for computing power,” and slower capital expenditure growth is not shrinking investment.

The market sees friction as a threat, Thorne contended, but “restraint prevents excess, cools the inflationary impulse and gives the AI boom more time to run.”

Friction Builds From Communities to Credit Markets

San Francisco recently imposed a 45-day moratorium on data center development, and President Donald Trump has urged developers to pay host communities a “dividend” to ease local opposition.

Credit markets are also getting choosier, Thorne argued.

Meta Platforms Inc.‘s (NASDAQ:META) five-year credit default swaps hit a record 114.79 basis points on Thursday, according to Markit data cited by Reuters.

CoreWeave Inc.‘s (NASDAQ:CRWV) 2031 bond yield reached a record 15.8%, according to TradingView.

More Years to Build, Less Strain

Spreading construction over more years, Thorne reasoned, eases the strain on equipment, labor and electricity infrastructure, giving suppliers time to expand and power systems time to catch up.

U.S. technology stocks plunged Thursday as concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) spending hammered Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA). However, Deepwater Asset Management’s Gene Munster maintained that the AI revolution remains in its early stages.

AI Spending Concerns Trigger Sharp Market Selloff

"Regarding the big AI selloff this week, we heard from Elon, Zuck, and Jensen that we’re still early, and I agree with them," Munster wrote on X, referencing to Space Exploration Technologies Corp.‘s (NASDAQ:SPCX) CEO Elon Musk, Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg, and Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang.

The Nasdaq Composite sank 2.6%, its steepest decline since June, while Meta dropped about 7%, Nvidia fell approximately 4%, and SpaceX tumbled around 9%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, the main benchmark for U.S.-listed chipmakers and closely tracked by the Invesco PHLX Semiconductor ETF (NYSE:SOXQ), plunged 6.7% as investors questioned AI infrastructure returns and financing costs.

On Wednesday, Meta reported $64.6 billion in quarterly revenue but posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion. It also projected 2026 capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion and announced plans to raise capital through nonvoting shares.

Read Also: Can a Weakening Jobs Report Slow Wall Street’s AI Slide?

Munster Sees Muse As Meta’s Future

Speaking on CNBC on Thursday, Munster argued that investors underestimate the potential of Meta’s personalized AI agents.

"Make no mistake, Muse is the future of the company," he said, describing autonomous commerce as its biggest opportunity.

Munster previously warned that Muse could threaten Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Google’s $250 billion search business, arguing that AI assistants could increasingly handle purchases directly. He estimated Muse had approximately 10 million daily users, although Meta has not disclosed that figure.

AI Agents Could Reshape Global Commerce

Munster predicted Meta’s infrastructure investments would continue climbing.

"We’re still not done with this build out," he said, estimating next year’s capital expenditures could exceed $225 billion. He also predicted that personal AI agents would transform advertising and shopping. "The future of marketing is not to humans. It’s bot to bot," Munster said.

His outlook follows earlier optimism about Nvidia’s AI infrastructure opportunity, including Huang’s expectations for growing computing demand. Munster also highlighted SpaceX’s expanding AI computing business, challenging concerns about excess capacity.

However, Reuters noted that Matthew Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak, offered a more cautious assessment Thursday, warning that investors were increasingly questioning returns on massive AI infrastructure investments. "It’s just becoming more and more evident to people that it’s going to take a lot longer," Maley said.

Spotify Technology S.A. (NYSE:SPOT) is embracing the rise of AI agents, betting that integrations with OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Meta Platforms, Inc.’s (NASDAQ:META) Muse and other assistants will expand access to its music catalog without weakening its relationship with listeners.

Spotify Wants to Be Everywhere In the AI Agent Race

Spotify shares closed Thursday up 11.19% at $583.66, despite the company missing Wall Street’s third-quarter earnings and revenue estimates, as subscriber and monthly active user growth supported investor sentiment.

The stock was down about 0.39% premarket on Friday, according to Benzinga Pro.

Co-CEO Gustav Söderström said during the earnings call that Spotify aims to become the preferred platform for licensed media across AI agents, allowing users to access music, podcasts and audiobooks through third-party assistants.

"We are simply everywhere," Söderström said, highlighting integrations with ChatGPT, Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses and Muse, as well as OpenAI’s Dots.

The strategy lets users request personalized playlists or discover audio content through AI assistants, while Spotify’s own systems handle recommendations and playback.

Söderström said the company is "unusually well positioned" for the agentic AI era because its subscription and advertising businesses can continue generating revenue even when listeners access Spotify in the background.

Its goal, Söderström said, is to become "the media service that you use from any agent," turning AI assistant growth into a business advantage.

The strategy could also give Spotify more insight into listeners’ preferences. Requests made through AI agents may reveal interests Spotify would not otherwise know, Söderström said, describing the resulting feedback loop as positive for the company.

He said Spotify does not share its proprietary user data with third-party agents. Instead, Spotify’s own systems handle requests and use available information to determine what to play.

Spotify is also developing AI-powered discovery tools and exploring paid features for AI-generated covers and remixes as it seeks to strengthen its own platform alongside external integrations.

NYU Stern finance professor Aswath “The Dean of Valuation” Damodaran warns that Anthropic’s upcoming IPO will be priced rather than valued. In his view, market dynamics, not intrinsic business worth, will set the number.

At an October 15 pre-IPO meeting in San Francisco, Anthropic reportedly posted third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion and an annualized revenue run rate (ARR) of $67 billion, seeing $100 billion by year-end.

Damodaran sees a familiar pattern. In the late 1990s, dot-com companies were priced on website visitors and then on “eyeballs,” a measure of time spent on sites. Now he sees ARR as the AI era’s version of that metric – a creative yardstick for companies whose financial statements can’t support their market prices.

Young Growth at Massive Scale

Under Damodaran’s life-cycle framework, Anthropic is a young growth company that happens to be enormous. Its very high revenue growth, operating losses, heavy reinvestment and negative cash flows are “features not bugs.”

However, he dismisses the company’s claim of an adjusted third-quarter profit.

“I don’t think even Anthropic believes it made money,” he said, and called adjusted figures “often a fictional number.” Free cash flow remains deeply negative.

Capital intensity is a big factor, as Anthropic has more than $400 billion in contractual compute commitments. Since the firm is still losing money and operates in a business environment just under formation, those obligations are real risks while investors have to price potential rather than proven cash flow.

See More: Top Momentum Stocks

The Murky Mathematics of ARR

Damodaran writes that ARR is “not standardized and can be easily gamed.” Companies can annualize from a day, a week, or a month of revenue. Both AI leaders currently use monthly figures, but “there is nothing that binds them to continue to do so.”

Accounting choices make comparisons harder. OpenAI switched to net revenue reporting, which cut its ARR from $70 billion to $50 billion. Anthropic still reports gross revenue and books cloud-provider payments as expenses.

At $1.5 trillion, Anthropic trades at about 23 times current ARR, but only five times a projected $300 billion in 2030 revenue.

“You’re going to see a lot of Anthropic bulls use forward numbers. Really, really forward numbers,” he predicted, “because it makes your metrics look more reasonable.”

The Peer Group Dilemma

Pricing depends on comparable companies, and almost no pure-play public LLM companies exist to compare against.

This approach pairs Anthropic with OpenAI, another private firm, so comparisons rely on stale venture rounds. The broader approach compares the firm with the Magnificent Seven and Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX), although these sharply differ in maturity, governance, and cash generation.

“Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) is a very different company than Anthropic,” Damodaran noted. Bears will argue that the gap in revenue and earnings “cannot be explained away with hope and potential.”

His core argument is that every pricing multiple hides a discounted cash flow model. 

“When you price companies, you’re making exactly the same assumptions I will have to make to value the company. You’re just making them implicitly,” he said.

In his view, to justify $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, Anthropic needs explosive revenue growth, operating margins of 30% or more, compute costs that grow more slowly than revenue and a risk profile that settles toward average as regulatory threats ease.

As cautious as ever, Damodaran sees the story as “a plausible one,” but warns that delivering on it is a whole different matter.

U.S. restrictions on high-bandwidth memory and semiconductor manufacturing equipment are limiting China’s ability to produce advanced AI chips, but experts warn the measures could also accelerate Beijing’s efforts to replace American technology.

HBM Shortage Creates Bottleneck For China’s AI Chips

In an exclusive statement to Benzinga, Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities, said the restrictions are having a dual effect, constraining Chinese chipmakers in the near term while encouraging domestic suppliers to develop alternatives.

"Every restriction also gives Chinese suppliers a larger captive market and stronger incentive to replace foreign technology," Boloor said.

Christopher Tang, a professor at the UCLA Anderson School of Management who studies global supply chains, told Benzinga that HBM is the most immediate constraint on China’s AI chip production.

China accumulated an estimated 13 million HBM stacks before U.S. controls took effect in December 2024, but those reserves are being depleted.

Domestic memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) is projected to produce about 2 million stacks in 2026, enough to support an estimated 250,000 to 300,000 Huawei Technologies Ascend-class chips, Tang said.

Without access to ASML Holding NV’s (NASDAQ:ASML) advanced extreme ultraviolet lithography equipment, Chinese manufacturers rely on older deep ultraviolet technology and multiple patterning techniques, which raise costs and reduce yields.

Tang said China could develop chips capable of meeting much of its domestic AI demand within a few years, though matching global leaders at scale could take until late this decade or beyond.

Read Also: Vertiv, Nvidia Target 30% More AI Token Output

Could US Chip Restrictions Backfire

The longer-term consequences could extend beyond China’s AI ambitions to American semiconductor companies.

Nvidia Corp’s (NASDAQ:NVDA) share of China’s AI accelerator market has effectively fallen to zero, Tang said.

He also noted that Applied Materials Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT) China revenue contribution declined to 28% from 35% a year earlier.

Beijing is further encouraging domestic substitution by requiring chipmakers to use at least 50% Chinese-made equipment when expanding capacity, Tang said.

While the global AI boom is currently helping offset some lost business, he warned that Chinese equipment suppliers could eventually become stronger international competitors.

"The long-term risk for the U.S. is that Chinese suppliers mature in a protected home market and then compete abroad," Tang said.

Boloor cautioned against assuming export restrictions will permanently strengthen U.S. chipmakers, arguing that limiting supply could ultimately push Chinese customers toward domestic alternatives.

Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comment. Intel Corp (NASDAQ:INTC) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (NYSE:TSM) declined to comment.

Nvidia Gets $35 Billion China Chip Orders

Earlier this week, it was reported that Nvidia has received chip orders worth more than $35 billion from Chinese tech giants ByteDance, Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. (NYSE:BABA) and Tencent Holdings Ltd. (OTC:TCEHY).

The companies reportedly ordered more than 3 million RTX PRO 5500 graphics cards at approximately $11,400 each.

According to MarketsandMarkets, China’s AI chip market was valued at $25.37 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $95.56 billion by 2030, representing a compound annual growth rate of 20.9%.

Munster Highlights Commerce Strength And AI-Agent Risk

Pony AI Inc. (NASDAQ:PONY) announced Friday that it signed a memorandum of understanding with NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and ride-hailing platform inDrive to explore autonomous ride-hailing services in Kazakhstan.

The companies will initially focus on Astana, the country’s capital, as they assess the technical, regulatory and commercial feasibility of deploying self-driving vehicles through the inDrive app.

NVIDIA Technology to Power Robotaxi Initiative

Under the agreement, Pony AI would supply its seventh-generation (Gen-7) robotaxis, while inDrive would operate the ride-hailing service.

Meanwhile, NVIDIA would provide artificial intelligence infrastructure to support the initiative.

The project will use NVIDIA Hyperion, a reference platform that combines sensors and computing technology for Level 4 autonomous vehicles.

NVIDIA’s robotaxi platform also integrates its Alpamayo software stack and Halos safety system to support autonomous driving.

Pony AI’s Gen-7 robotaxis feature multiple sensors, redundant systems and technology designed to maintain operations during certain system failures.

The company already operates fully driverless commercial services in major Chinese cities. It has also deployed autonomous driving technology across Europe, the Middle East and Asia.

Kazakhstan Emerges As Initial Test Market

The companies selected Kazakhstan following the introduction of the country’s first structured legal framework for driverless transportation.

The initiative aligns with Kazakhstan’s efforts to advance digitalization and artificial intelligence adoption.

Pony AI and inDrive plan to introduce robotaxis in Astana, subject to an agreement with the Kazakh government.

The city has approximately 1.7 million residents, providing a potential market for autonomous transportation services.

Additionally, inDrive’s existing operations in Kazakhstan could help support the proposed rollout.

Expansion Plans Depend on Initial Results

Following the planned Astana launch, the companies will evaluate opportunities to expand into other Kazakh cities and international markets where inDrive operates.

However, the agreement remains exploratory, and the companies have not announced a launch date.

The collaboration could help Pony AI expand its international footprint as it seeks to commercialize autonomous driving technology beyond China.

The typical S&P 500 company is having its best month against the index in more than 17 years. The index itself, however, has barely moved.

That gap is the clearest sign yet that money is leaving the artificial intelligence trade and spreading across the rest of the market.

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSE:RSP), which gives every company in the index the same weight, has gained 4.9% in October through Thursday’s close. Meanwhile, the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:SPY), dominated by the largest technology names, is up just 0.2%.

As a result, the ratio between the two funds has climbed 4.7% this month. That is the biggest relative monthly jump since April 2009, when stocks were rebounding from the financial crisis lows.

The rotation has also flipped the year-to-date scoreboard. The equal-weight ETF is now up 13.5% in 2026, ahead of the 11.4% gain for SPY.

Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF relative to the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF, monthly change. Source: TradingView

Thursday showed the shift in a single session.

The equal-weight ETF rose 0.7%, while the S&P 500 fell 1.2% as Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) tumbled 7% on concerns about its AI spending. Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) lost 4.4%.

The State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE:XLK) dropped 3.3%. By contrast, the State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE:XLP) jumped 3.3% and the State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE:XLU) added 2.1%.

Investors Are Questioning Who Pays for the AI Build-Out

Bank of America Global Research strategist Sebastian Raedler said in a report Friday that there are “mounting signs of markets becoming increasingly unwilling to fund the AI infrastructure build-out.”

In Europe, according to Raedler, cyclical sectors have trailed defensive ones by 11%, the sharpest rotation since the COVID-19 shock of March 2020.

He also pointed to Ramp data showing that AI spending by U.S. businesses has stopped rising in recent months as token prices decline.

At 22V Research, Dennis DeBusschere said the market’s reflex on days when AI capex worries flare has been to buy banks, retailers, small caps, housing and transport stocks.

However, he drew a line between near-term and long-term risk.

“AI capex concerns are about 2028 and beyond. NOT 2027,” DeBusschere said, adding that investors remain highly confident 2027 spending plans will be met.

Is the Rotation Now Over? This Year’s Spikes Faded Fast

History offers two very different answers.

After April 2009, the equal-weight ETF kept going. Over the following 12 months, the RSP-to-SPY ratio rose another 9.4%.

This year, the pattern has been the opposite. In February, the ratio jumped 4.4% in a single month, then gave back 7.6% over the next three months.

A 3.2% gain in June was followed by a 4.3% decline through September.

There is also a key difference with 2009.

Back then, the average stock led because almost everything was rising. In October 2026, it is leading largely because the giants are falling, with defensive sectors doing much of the heavy lifting.

John Roque, also of 22V Research, sees that as a warning rather than a green light. As of Thursday morning, new lows had outnumbered new highs on the NYSE and Nasdaq for 37 and 38 straight sessions, respectively, even though the S&P 500 was only a little more than 1% below its record.

According to Roque, Nasdaq data going back to 2015 shows nine prior streaks of at least 33 days of net new lows. In seven of them, the Nasdaq went on to fall at least 18%.

He also noted that most major U.S. banks are trading below their 200-day moving averages, warning that “when banks / financials are not strong, you cannot have a strong market.”

With six trading sessions left in October, the equal-weight fund is on track for a historic month.

Whether it marks the start of a broader advance, as in 2009, or a defensive retreat from AI will depend on whether the rest of the market can keep rising once the selling in megacaps stops.

Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) is in the spotlight Friday, with the stock closing in on Nvidia Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) as the world’s most valuable company, the iPhone Duo hitting stores today and earnings a week and a half away all drawing attention.

  • Apple stock is approaching key resistance levels. Why did AAPL hit a new high?

Apple Is $42 Billion Behind Nvidia in the Race to Be the World’s Most Valuable Company

Apple closed at a record $348.22 Thursday, putting its market value at $5.082 trillion, just $42 billion behind Nvidia at $5.124 trillion, according to 24/7 Wall St. A gain of about 0.83% would close the gap. Apple last closed above Nvidia on July 27, and it first topped $5 trillion on Oct. 14. Nvidia’s lead was about $903 billion on Oct. 6, and Benzinga reported it had shrunk by nearly $570 billion in six trading sessions as concerns about the cost of the AI build-out weighed on the chip maker. Apple’s restrained AI infrastructure spending may be working in its favor, Benzinga said.

Tough reviews of the foldable iPhone Duo haven’t shaken Apple’s bulls, according to Yahoo Finance. 24/7 Wall St. noted that Apple trades at about twice Nvidia’s forward price-to-earnings ratio, so a market-cap lead could prove short-lived.

The iPhone Duo, Apple’s First Foldable, Hits Stores Today

The iPhone Duo goes on sale today after pre-orders sold out within moments on Oct. 16 and shipping dates slipped to Nov. 16 and Nov. 23, according to AppleInsider. It said Apple is believed to have made fewer iPhone Duos than normal, so the sellout is harder to read, but that stores will have at least some stock today. The phone will not appear in Apple’s fiscal fourth quarter, which ended Sept. 26.

Apple to Report Fiscal Fourth-Quarter Results Nov. 2

Apple is due to report its fourth-quarter results after the market closes on Nov. 2. Analysts estimate earnings per share of $1.98 on revenue of $113.23 billion. Apple has guided to revenue growth of 9% to 11% and a gross margin of 47% to 48%. In the third quarter, Apple reported earnings per share of $2.02, beating the consensus estimate of $1.89, and revenue of $109.42 billion, beating the consensus estimate of $108.65 billion.

What to Watch: December Quarter Outlook, iPhone Demand and Margins

Investors will be closely tracking Apple’s December-quarter guidance, since the iPhone Duo launches in it and sales of the iPhone 18 Pro, which Apple launched in September, will run the full quarter. JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee expects December-quarter earnings per share of $2.81, about 4% below the consensus estimate of $2.92, and about 8.5 million iPhone Duo units. Gross margin will also be in focus.

Apple guided to 47% to 48% for the fourth quarter, down from 50.1% in the third quarter, which included about 2 points from tariff refunds, while citing memory costs and supply constraints. Services growth and any update on the planned December launch of Apple Intelligence in China will also be watched.

China’s reported $2.5 billion-a-day equity ETF buying spree is raising a bigger question for investors: Could the U.S. Federal Reserve eventually use ETFs to stabilize stocks during the next major market selloff?

Eric Balchunas, senior ETF analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said China’s government has been buying roughly $2.5 billion in equity ETFs daily since July, following an artificial intelligence-driven market slump. That is about 11.5 times the typical daily ETF flow of $218 million cited by Balchunas. He likened the scale to the U.S. Treasury buying $100 billion of ETFs every day.

Balchunas has previously argued that the Federal Reserve could eventually follow a similar approach, with China and Japan helping normalize government-backed equity purchases. He believes such intervention could become more common over the next five to 10 years.

China’s ETF Purchases Are More Than a Market Signal

China’s state-backed investor Central Huijin Investment has been a key player in the country’s market-support efforts, using ETFs to channel capital into domestic equities.

Bloomberg Intelligence estimates that Central Huijin redeployed $43 billion into equities after purchases resumed in July 2026. It had about $188 billion in available funds remaining, according to Livemint. The buying has included broad-market exposure through funds tracking the CSI 300 Index, alongside greater allocations to technology-focused benchmarks.

However, state buying does not guarantee a sustained recovery. Bloomberg Intelligence has cautioned that intervention may slow a selloff without reversing it when investor sentiment and underlying fundamentals remain weak.

Japan Has Already Crossed That Line

The Bank of Japan built substantial equity ETF holdings through a 2010 program and expanded them during its monetary-easing campaign. In March 2024, it discontinued new ETF purchases.

In September 2025, it announced plans to gradually dispose of its holdings, showing that central-bank equity ownership can become a long-term policy and balance-sheet issue.

Could the Fed Become an Equity ETF Buyer?

A future U.S. intervention would represent a significant departure from conventional Federal Reserve operations. The Fed’s statutory mandate centers on maximum employment and stable prices, not directly supporting stock valuations.

Any move toward equity ETF purchases would raise questions about its legal authority, financial independence, market distortions and the distribution of gains among investors.

For ETF investors, the implication is not that a U.S. rescue is imminent. Instead, China and Japan provide precedents for how governments and central banks might use ETFs to stabilize markets during severe downturns.

The next major bear market could test whether that approach remains largely an Asian policy tool or becomes part of a broader global debate.
